summary: An informational RFC from IBM describing the thinking behind Network/440, an experimental computer networking project at IBM Research in Yorktown Heights. The project aimed to understand networking, find design problems and implement solutions.

eli5.summary: A company explains how its own small test network was designed and what they learned, to share ideas with the ARPANET builders.

questions: what did ibm research learn from its network project
what is the logical network machine
how did network/440 handle flow control
subtitle: IBM's design philosophy for computer networks and protocols.

tldr.problem: Early computer networks required design decisions about how to handle message routing, error recovery, flow control, and resource management across multiple independent systems.
tldr.mechanism: IBM's Network/440 project proposed a protocol architecture with two major functions: the Network Controller (NC) for job-level management, and the Express Exchange (EE) for message handling and switching, separated from user data transmission.
tldr.outcome: The protocol concepts proved feasible in IBM's operational networks and influenced thinking about network design in the ARPANET era.

facts.label: Project location
facts.value: IBM Thomas J. Watson Research Center, Yorktown Heights, NY

today: RFC 187 presents IBM's thinking on network design and protocol architecture from the early 1970s. The logical network machine concept and the separation of control and communication functions influenced how networks were designed and remain relevant to modern distributed systems.

sections.title: The Logical Network Machine
sections.content:
Network/440 is an experimental computer networking project undertaken by IBM Research to understand networking problems and implement solutions. The project's core philosophy is the concept of a logical network machine: treating all systems involved in the network as parts of a single large multiprocessor system, even though they are physically distributed.

Rather than viewing the network as merely connecting separate computers, the logical network machine approach treats the entire network as a unified computing platform. This abstraction lets programmers think of the network as having a single operating system, simplifying application development.
sections.eli5: Instead of thinking of the network as separate computers sending messages, think of it as one giant computer made of many parts far apart.

sections.title: Network Control and Message Exchange
sections.content:
The protocol defines two major functions that can exist on any system in any physical configuration. The Network Controller (NC) is a higher-level function that manages network jobs and their execution across the system. It controls job initiation, execution flow, and file transfers between systems.

The Express Exchange (EE) is a communication handler and store-and-forward switch that moves messages between stations without NC overhead. This separation lets fast routine messages flow directly through the EE while important control messages go through the NC. The architecture is flexible enough to work in distributed networks (where the EE directly routes messages) or star networks (with centralized NC and EE).
sections.eli5: The network has a mail handler (EE) that quickly sends regular messages, and a manager (NC) that handles big decisions like which files to move and when.

sections.title: Message Structure and Control
sections.content:
Every message in Network/440 consists of a header and text. The header contains operational functions including: an Action Code that routes the message to the right destination, a Transmission Block Number to detect lost messages, a Network Job Identifier to track which job the message belongs to, and Logical Message Flags that mark the first and last blocks of multi-block messages.

The protocol includes selective flow control: systems can halt transmission of all messages for a job, or just specific logical messages, while always reserving buffer space for interrupt messages. When files are too large to fit in available buffers, the EE can store them on disk as a logical extension of core memory.
sections.eli5: Each message has labels saying where it goes and which job it belongs to. If a computer gets too full, it can ask the sender to wait, but urgent messages always get through.

references.text: McKay, D. B., Karp, D. P., "A Network/440 Protocol Concept", RFC 187, July 1971.
